entries.title: I Peter 3:2
segments: Coupled with fear See note on

entries.title: I Peter 3:3
segments: Braiding the hair, etc.  This was a warning against the extravagant fashions in hair-dressing and decoration with costly jewels, prevailing among the Greeks and Romans at that period; also a reminder that the true adornment is from within.

entries.title: I Peter 3:4
segments: Meek and quiet spirit. This implies meekness as toward God, the fountain of all knowledge; and perfect calmness in that knowledge, as toward men.

entries.title: I Peter 3:7
segments: That your prayers be not hindered. Lest your approach to God in prayer lack humility and prove unacceptable by reason of your overbearing conduct to those who are weaker than you.

entries.title: I Peter 3:15
segments:
Ready always to give answer. This is an admonition toward understanding; something more than blind faith was required.
 

 
 With meekness and fear. The attitude here urged by the apostle is one devoid of boastfulness, and at the same time guarded by an anxious fear lest in the smallest particular we fail to meet fully the situation.

entries.title: I Peter 3:19
segments:
, 20
 
 In which also he went and preached, etc.  The interpretation of these two verses depends on whether the word 'spirit' in 1Pe 3.18 refers to the Holy Spirit, or to the eternal element in man which Jesus shared in his human nature.  There are several interpretations, of which the two most important are: (1) that Christ actually descended into Hades and preached to the people who had lived in the days of Noah but were now in Hades; (2) that the Spirit of Christ preached through Noah to those who lived in Noah's time but who were in prison at the time of the writing of this epistle.  Commentators differ widely as to the correct interpretation.

entries.title: I Peter 3:21
segments:
Doth now save you, even baptism. Noah's experience in the flood is made a type of baptism.  Through faith Noah obeyed God and was saved when others were lost. Some would interpret this experience  as being typical of the symbolism of baptism, while others would interpret it as meaning that we are actually saved through baptism. The verse must be interpreted in connection with other passages of scripture.
 

 
 Not the putting away, etc.  The interpretation of this passage is unusually difficult.  What is the first question that a newly made believer asks? Paul asked, What shall I do, Lord? (

).  The answer to this question is, Surrender yourself to Christ; become dead to the world and the old life.  Baptism is a symbol of this surrender; it is an act of obedience.  Peter emphasizes this by showing the difference between Christian baptism and the Jewish washings.
